name: Assumed similarity bias
statement: People judging a stranger's personality import their own self-description into the judgement, and the effect persists after the stranger's observed behaviour is controlled.
meaning: The measure is a correlation, not an estimate about a population. A perceiver describes their own personality, describes a target, and the two descriptions are compared across items or traits. In the Social Relations Model the same idea is fitted across a group: assumed similarity is the correlation between a person's own standing on a trait and their perceiver effect, which is how they rate everyone on average. The claim is that the first description leaks into the second. It is separable from actual similarity, because the target's own self-report can be entered as a control. It is also separable from the false consensus effect, entry 10, which asks for the percentage of a population sharing a two-way choice and then compares that percentage between people who chose differently.

origin.note: Cronbach did not coin the phrase. His own reference list gives Fiedler's 1954 paper on assumed similarity measures as the example of the formula, and he notes Fiedler's ASo variant, computed between two others rather than between self and other. What Cronbach added was the algebra that took the score apart. The version read for this entry is the August 1954 technical report of the same title, issued as report no. 10 by the Group Effectiveness Research Laboratory at the University of Illinois under an Office of Naval Research contract, with Fiedler as principal investigator.

evidence: Cronbach defines the assumed similarity score as the sum, over items, of squared differences between a judge's rating of another person and that judge's rating of himself. He splits it into four terms: assumed elevation, assumed dispersion in elevation, assumed self-typicality, and assumed dispersion within items. The first pair asks whether the judge places others at his own average level on the scale. The second pair asks whether the judge treats his own profile shape as typical. The same components sit inside accuracy scores, so a correlation between measured empathy and measured projection follows from the arithmetic. Cronbach's verdict on one published set of such correlations is that they would arise even where both sets of responses are determined strictly by chance, and that they have no psychological meaning. His illustrative decomposition uses eight judges. Hughes, Flournoy and Srivastava tested the modern version in 2021. 322 previously unacquainted people self-reported on the Big Five Inventory 2, met a stranger the next day for a 20-minute art gallery task, and afterwards rated that stranger. Their model estimates the direct path from a perceiver's own trait to their perception of the partner, holding the partner's coded behaviour constant. That path was positive in all five domains and in 9 of 15 facets. Agreeableness was the largest, an unstandardised 0.197 with a 95% interval of 0.116 to 0.285, standardised at .25. The other four ran from .16 for neuroticism down to .10 for extraversion.

replication.headline: A preregistered dyadic study of 322 strangers found assumed similarity in all five Big Five domains, largest for agreeableness at a standardised path of .25, with the partner's actual behaviour held constant.
replication.detail: Hughes, Flournoy and Srivastava separate three routes to perceived similarity, and the traditional one survives. Alongside it, behaviour expressed during the interaction predicted perceptions of the partner beyond stable traits, at standardised .11 for agreeableness, .10 for energy level and .17 for neuroticism. A double-mediated path, in which a perceiver expresses a trait, draws matching behaviour out of the partner, and then reads that behaviour accurately, was supported for sociability and for openness at .02 each, and ran the other way for assertiveness at -.02. For agreeableness that compound path was 0.001, 95% interval -0.002 to 0.005. Part of what looks assumed is therefore elicited, and the authors call every compound effect small. Kenny and West's meta-analysis of 24 studies is the standing summary of the correlational literature, and it is paywalled; only its abstract was read here, at PubMed. Kenny's own summary page puts the correlation of self-perception with the perception of one other at .25, against .27 for the similarity a perceiver sees between two others, and states the second is statistically the larger. Those two figures are quoted from that page rather than from the paper, and they are not in the fields above.

study.cite: Hughes, B. T., Flournoy, J. C., & Srivastava, S. (2021). Is perceived similarity more than assumed similarity? An interpersonal path to seeing similarity between self and others. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 121(1), 184-200.

limits: Cronbach's illustrative analysis rests on eight judges, and he writes that correlations based on eight cases cannot be interpreted confidently. His paper is algebra: he says so, describing the method as almost entirely algebraic analysis based on a model rather than on behaviour. The Hughes study is one laboratory, one 20-minute task and one sample of previously unacquainted people, and its authors treat the compound paths as suggestive rather than as a basis for strong conclusions. The Kenny and West figures were not read off the paper. A larger problem sits under any raw similarity score, and Wood and Furr set it out. Most of an overall profile similarity is the normative profile, the description that fits almost anybody. In their roommate sample the average overall similarity was .68, and the average distinctive similarity, after subtracting the normative profile from both sides, was .10. The two rankings of the same people correlated .42. Overall similarity, personality stability and judgement agreement all correlated with one another at .26 or above; the distinctive versions correlated at .08 or below in absolute value. Overall roommate similarity correlated .28 with satisfaction with life, and distinctive similarity -.01. Their correlations rest on between 93 and 151 people. Searches of Crossref, Europe PMC and OSF found no multi-laboratory replication of the Social Relations Model estimate of assumed similarity.
misreadings: The name promises an error and the measure does not deliver one. Where the target really does resemble the perceiver, a self-anchored judgement is a correct judgement. Hughes and colleagues make the sharper version of the point: in a live interaction a perceiver can produce the similarity they then perceive, so some of the correlation is elicited rather than assumed. It is not the false consensus effect, entry 10, although the two are filed together and Kenny lists false consensus among the names assumed similarity travels under. False consensus compares the population estimates of two groups who chose differently on a two-way item, and needs no target. Assumed similarity correlates one person's self-description with their description of a particular other person, and needs no second group. Nor is it psychological projection, entry 43, whose Freudian sense requires the perceiver to be denying the trait. The last error is to read the raw number as a quantity of bias. Wood and Furr's roommate figures, .68 overall against .10 distinctive, are the size of the gap between the two readings.

sources.text: Cronbach, L. J. (1955). Processes affecting scores on "understanding of others" and "assumed similarity." Psychological Bulletin, 52(3), 177-193. The version read for this entry is the August 1954 University of Illinois technical report of the same title, scanned at the Internet Archive; the published article is paywalled.

Fiedler, F. E. (1954). Assumed similarity measures as predictors of team effectiveness. The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 49(3), 381-388. Cited by Cronbach as the example of the assumed similarity formula; not read for this entry.

Cronbach, L. J., & Gleser, G. C. (1953). Assessing similarity between profiles. Psychological Bulletin, 50(6), 456-473. The profile-distance paper Cronbach's decomposition builds on; not read for this entry.

Kenny, D. A., & West, T. V. (2010). Similarity and agreement in self- and other perception: A meta-analysis. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 14(2), 196-213. Abstract read at PubMed; the full text is paywalled and no open copy was located.
